Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "please help me revise this plan for the family photo catalogue so it reads clearly for the relatives who will be helping. we are making a searchable catalogue of photographs kept by the Morgan family, not a new family history book. the boxes are in the upstairs hall closet at Elaine Morgan's house, and the albums are currently split between Elaine and her brother Peter. The working catalogue should include scanned pictures and a record for items we cannot scan yet. We want people to find a photograph by date, place, person, or event, even when we only know some of those details. It should also be possible to see which details are guesses instead of confirmed information.

The first sorting day is planned for Saturday, October 12, from 10 a.m. until 3 p.m., at Elaine's house. Peter will bring the three albums he has, and Elaine will set out the four boxes from the closet. Their cousin Ruth can only come for the first two hours, so the work should not depend on her being there all day. We expect around six relatives in total, but nobody has confirmed the final number. There is one dining table available for sorting, and the scanner will be on a small desk in the den. Please leave enough room for people to move between those spaces. The kitchen table is not available because Elaine will use it for lunch.

We have agreed to start with the photographs from the 1940s through the 1970s, since those are the ones most often requested by relatives. Some prints are loose, and others are attached to album pages with corners or old adhesive. Nobody should pull a photograph off a page if it does not lift easily. If a picture can be removed without force, scan it at the highest setting the scanner supports and put it back in its original place afterward. If it cannot be removed safely, photograph the whole page instead, and make a note that the image is a page photograph rather than a scan of the print. We do not want to damage an album just to get a cleaner digital image.

For each image, the catalogue needs an item number, the file name, the best known date, the location if known, names of people who can be identified, and the event or occasion if anyone knows it. Add the source too, such as “Elaine, blue album” or “Peter, box 2,” so we can return to the original. The item number should stay with the image even if we later correct its date or names. We have not decided whether to use full dates or year-only dates when the month and day are not known, so please make the date field flexible enough for either. Do not turn an approximate date into a confirmed one. A note like “about 1956, based on the car” is useful, but it should not look like a documented date.

1. The person doing the scan should enter the item number and file name before moving on to the next picture. Use a file name that starts with the item number, then a short description, for example “FM-0142_family-picnic.” Do not use a person's name in the file name unless someone in the group has identified that person with confidence. This should reduce the chance of a wrong name being copied into several places. If the picture has no known people, still give it an item number and describe what can be seen, such as “two bicycles by a fence.”

2. Keep a separate list of possible identifications when the group is unsure. We have a photograph of a woman standing beside the porch at the Lake Road house, and Elaine thinks it might be her aunt Nora, but Peter is not sure. The catalogue should say “unidentified woman, possibly Nora Morgan” and explain that Elaine suggested the name. It should not list Nora as a confirmed person. If someone later finds a labeled copy or another reliable clue, we can update the record and keep the earlier note in the change history. Please do not erase uncertainty just because the catalogue looks neater without it.

3. For pictures with several people, record names from left to right only when the group can agree on the order. If relatives disagree about who is in a photograph, leave the disputed name out of the confirmed-people field and describe the disagreement in a note. For example, two relatives remember the man in the 1962 picnic photograph differently; one says Uncle James and the other says their neighbor Mr. Cole. We should record both suggestions, with who made each suggestion, instead of choosing one for now. A person who is present at sorting can write their own name beside a suggestion, but that does not automatically make it confirmed.

Please mark any photograph that appears fragile, torn, damp, or stuck to another photograph, and do not scan it until Elaine has looked at it. Put it in a clean paper sleeve, with its item number written on a separate slip rather than on the photograph. The same applies to images with writing on the back: scan both sides if they can be handled safely, and enter the writing as a transcription, keeping the original spelling where it is readable. If the writing is hard to make out, use “[unclear]” for the part we cannot read rather than guessing. We may need to ask another relative about names or places written in older handwriting.

The catalogue will be kept in a shared spreadsheet at first. Elaine will hold the original albums and boxes, while Peter will keep a backup copy of the image files on an external drive. If the family later chooses a different storage service, the item numbers and file names should remain the same so links can be updated without renaming every image. Do not upload photographs to a public website during this first stage. We have not discussed permission for that, and several pictures show children who are still living. Relatives should be able to use the shared catalogue, but only Elaine and Peter should have permission to change the main records until we agree on another arrangement.

Before the sorting day, ask relatives to bring any dates or names they already know, but make clear that no one needs to prepare a complete list. Elaine has a short list of weddings and birthdays from the old family calendar, and Peter has two envelopes labeled “Rochester trip” and “Grandma’s garden.” Those labels may help with sorting, but they do not prove that every photograph in an envelope belongs to that event. If an envelope label conflicts with handwriting on a photograph or with a well-supported family memory, record both pieces of information and flag the record for later review. Do not silently use the envelope label as the answer.

At the end of the day, leave unsorted items grouped by their original box or album, and put the item-number slips in the same group. The scan files and spreadsheet should be copied to Peter's external drive before everyone leaves, if the files can be checked against the item list that day. Otherwise, keep the files on the den computer and make a note of which items still need a backup; do not claim that a backup exists until Peter has checked it. The next sorting session is not scheduled yet.
